source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: On GPQA Diamond, a step-by-step instruction helps non-reasoning models on average, but adds almost nothing to dedicated reasoning models and costs 20 to 80 percent more time.
numbers: 198 questions x 25 runs per condition. Non-reasoning, average change in accuracy (risk difference): Gemini Flash 2.0 +0.135 vs direct, +0.062 vs default. Reasoning models, step-by-step vs direct: o3-mini +0.029 (p=.024), o4-mini +0.031 (p=.003), Gemini Flash 2.5 -0.033 (p=.005). Time up 20 to 80 percent (10 to 20 s) for reasoning models.
quote: For dedicated reasoning models, the added benefits of explicit CoT prompting appear negligible
limits: One benchmark (GPQA Diamond, multiple choice). Tests a plain step-by-step instruction, not step-back or abstraction. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Models are 2025 versions.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 9. On a reasoning model a scaffold step that only asks for more thinking buys about 3 points at best. The gate in S0 should assume that extra reasoning prompts have near-zero value on strong models unless shown otherwise on our own tasks.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
finding: The authors report that giving worked examples in the prompt hurts their reasoning model, and tell users to describe the problem and output format zero-shot.
numbers: No table. Stated as a prompt-engineering observation in the discussion of evaluation.
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: Vendor statement with no numbers or ablation. One model family. Does not test comparison of two cases or a derived rule, only plain demonstrations.
agent_relevance: Gap 1. Any S2 induction step that pastes cases into the prompt may lower accuracy on a reasoning-trained model. The human recipe must be tested against a zero-shot arm, and cases should be kept out unless they beat it.

source: Xu, Xie, Zhao, He (2025) Chain of Draft: Thinking Faster by Writing Less
finding: Asking for very short reasoning steps (about five words each) keeps most of the chain-of-thought gain at a fraction of the tokens. This is the nearest published test of a short plain answer against a long one.
numbers: GSM8K, few-shot. GPT-4o: standard 53.3 percent, CoT 95.4, CoD 91.1. Claude 3.5 Sonnet: standard 64.6, CoT 95.8, CoD 91.4. CoD uses about 40 tokens per response, an 80 percent cut vs CoT (about 200). Authors also report a 92.4 percent token cut on one other task.
limits: Few-shot setup; authors say zero-shot CoD is weaker and small models (1.5B to 3B) lose more. Two 2024 models. Only the GSM8K row was read closely.
agent_relevance: Gap 2. At a fixed small token budget, terse reasoning loses about 4 points to long CoT but beats no reasoning by 27 to 38 points. Any scaffold that claims a gain must beat a terse-reasoning arm of the same length, not only a bare answer.

source: Guo, Gu, Jin, Spanos, Lavaei (2026) StyleBench: Evaluating thinking styles in Large Language Models
finding: Across 5 reasoning styles, 5 tasks and 15 open models (270M to 120B), more structure helps only on hard open-ended search tasks and only for large models. On simple tasks plain chain of thought is best or ties.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT best in every capacity regime. Knowledge task (CommonsenseQA): all styles converge for large models. Qwen-7B strategy-selection study, averaged over 5 tasks: CoT 50.2, SFT selector 53.3, GRPO selector 58.8 (other columns garbled in the text layer). Search styles use more and more variable tokens.
limits: Open models only, no frontier closed models. AoT here means Algorithm-of-Thought, not Abstraction-of-Thought. Table text is garbled; only the stated findings are used.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 9. Supports a gate: structured scaffolds pay on hard combinatorial tasks with a capable model, and not on easy or knowledge-bound tasks. Learning which style to use is itself hard (SFT collapsed to shallow preferences).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures (re-opened to check)
finding: Confirms the correction: gains are largest on tasks that need world knowledge and moderate on algorithmic tasks. Gains over CoT shrink a lot on the strongest model for math.
numbers: PaLM 2-L: BBH 56 direct, 60 CoT, 67 Self-Discover; T4D 30/40/69; MATH 45/42/50.5. GPT-4: BBH 58/75/81; T4D 51/52/85; MATH 70.5/71/73. So over CoT on GPT-4: +6 BBH, +33 T4D, +2 MATH. Cost: 3 extra calls per task class, then 1 call per instance, 10 to 40 times fewer calls than CoT with self-consistency.
quote: SELF-DISCOVER performs best on tasks that require diverse world knowledge
limits: Older models (PaLM 2-L, GPT-4 of 2023). Setup calls not counted per instance. Prompt is longer than CoT, so tokens are not equal. T4D is a task the authors' structure fits well.
agent_relevance: Gap 2. Per-class structure is cheap to amortise but the gain on the stronger model for math (+2) is small. Count setup tokens under G7.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (re-opened: ablations)
finding: Rule-built workflows (de-duplicated, executable action sequences) match model-written workflows on WebArena and trail slightly on Mind2Web. Retrieving whole past examples (Synapse) is worse than either.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4): rule 35.6 success, 6.3 steps vs LM 35.5, 5.9 steps. Mind2Web cross-task: MindAct 41.6 element acc / 36.2 step SR / 2.0 SR; rule 49.5 / 43.4 / 2.0; LM 50.6 / 45.1 / 4.8. Versus Synapse (retrieved concrete examples): +5.0 element accuracy and +4.0 step success. Code vs text workflow format: text +0.6 element acc, +0.3 step SR, -1.2 task SR (no real difference).
limits: Authors' own settings. Synapse differs in more than abstraction (different prompt, no sub-routines). LM-induction win on Mind2Web (+1.7 step SR, +2.8 task SR over rule) shows model abstraction helps somewhat when contexts vary. Single benchmark family.
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Most of the gain comes from storing validated routines, not from clever abstraction, but a small extra comes from model-side abstraction of example-specific details. Cheap rule-based routine stores are a fair baseline.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: On the same agent and tasks, raw trajectory memory, workflow memory and distilled strategy memory form a ladder, with distilled strategies from successes and failures best.
numbers: WebArena overall success, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5, Synapse (raw trajectories) 42.1, AWM (workflows) 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8, plus test-time scaling 51.8. Multi-site subset: AWM 3.4 vs no memory 10.3 (AWM hurts), ReasoningBank 13.8. Number of retrieved experiences: success is highest at 1 and falls to 44.4 at 4 (45.5 at 3). Adding failures: Synapse 40.6 to 41.7, AWM 44.4 to 42.2, ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7 (Shopping, flash).
limits: Authors' own method; baselines re-run by them. Distillation also changes what is stored (failures, strategies), so 'abstraction' is confounded with 'content'. Retrieval count curve is from one subset and its text layer is partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 6. More retrieved cases is not better for agents (1 best, 4 worst). Abstraction adds 2 to 5 points over raw reuse, but only when it also learns from failures. Cross-site transfer is where simple workflow stores fail.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky, Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory
finding: A curated, rewritten memory of tips and code snippets beats both no memory and raw retrieval of past answers. The largest jumps come from a stored, runnable routine, not from a stated principle.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4o: baseline 10, instructions only 19, raw retrieval 6, curated memory (DC-Cu) 93, curated plus retrieval (DC-RS) 99. Claude 3.5 Sonnet on the same task: 12/10/11/14/14 (it never adopted the code routine). AIME 2024, Claude: baseline 23.3, instructions only 36.7, raw retrieval 43.3, DC-Cu 50.0, DC-RS 46.7. Full-history appending: Claude 26.7, GPT-4o 6.7 (vs DC 40 to 50). GPQA Diamond Claude 59.6 to 68.7; GPT-4o 57.1 to 58.1.
limits: 2024 to 2025 models. Part of the AIME gain (13 of 27 points for Claude) comes from the added instructions (DC-) with no memory. Order of questions is fixed. Results are model-specific: Claude missed the code routine.
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Test arms for memory: raw solved cases vs curated tips vs executable routine. Executable, validated routines carry most of the effect; raw retrieval can be worse than none. Also shows that a strong instruction prompt alone is a big confound.

source: Yang et al. (2026) PlugMem: A Task-Agnostic Plugin Memory Module for LLM Agents
finding: Ablation: turning raw episodes into structured knowledge (facts and skills) beats plain chunking of the same episodes on long-memory QA, multi-hop QA and web tasks. Retrieval matters most.
numbers: LongMemEval accuracy: full 75.1, no structuring (turn-level chunks) 62.8, no retrieval 57.2. HotpotQA EM/F1: full 61.4/74.1, no structuring 51.4/62.0, no retrieval 20.0/24.3. WebArena (online/offline success): Shopping 52.6/58.4 full vs 50.0/51.7 no structuring; GitLab 51.4/55.2 vs 41.7/42.0; Multi-site 20.0/21.6 vs 20.0/18.4.
limits: Authors' own system. 'No structuring' removes more than abstraction (it also changes the index), so the effect is not purely abstraction. WebArena gap is small on Shopping online.
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Gives a size for abstraction at the memory layer, 10 to 12 points on QA memory tasks, but retrieval quality dominates. Do not credit abstraction for what the index does.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models (re-opened: ARC arm)
finding: GPT-4 states rules in words, then writes programs. In ARC a program that passed the shown examples almost always passed the hidden test, so an executed rule is a good check of a written rule. Summarising the rule list lost some.
numbers: 100 ARC tasks: direct 17, program only 23, summarised hypotheses 30, human-selected hypotheses 33, human-written (LARC) hypotheses 45. GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks; of 30 solved with summaries, 28 had a correct hypothesis before summarising. Only 33 of the 49 tasks (67 percent) with a correct hypothesis led to a correct program. Summary vs human selection: 30 vs 33 tasks (about 9 percent relative loss in this table). Only one task in ARC where a train-passing program failed the test.
limits: This paper does not give the 26 percent loss that claim K20 quotes; that figure is from the list-function study (Parab et al.). The two studies disagree on how reliable train-passing is (ARC: almost always; list functions: 45.4 percent fail). Domain and number of examples decide it.
agent_relevance: Gap 4. A stated rule is worth little until it is run on all examples and on a held-out instance. Rule wording quality alone does not predict transfer in models; execution does. Do not summarise the candidate list before testing.

source: Puranam, Sen, Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs Help Improve Analogical Reasoning For Strategic Decisions? (re-opened with tables)
finding: With two source stories and two target problems, GPT-4 never named the correct source unprompted, and with a hint it claimed to use both sources almost always. It did not reliably choose the right case. No condition forced a causal-structure check, so the question stays open.
numbers: GPT-4, 15 runs per cell. No hint: correct analogy used 0 of 15 for both targets (precision, recall, F1 all 0, accuracy 0.50 to 0.54). With hint: Radiation target TP 15, FP 14, TN 1, precision 0.52, recall 1.00, F1 0.68, accuracy 0.53; Dolphin target TP 15, FP 15, precision 0.50. Humans (N=46 per target): no hint precision 0.42 and 1.00, recall 0.06 and 0.22; with hint precision 0.67 and 0.75, recall 0.26 and 0.39. Humans solving: factory 6.3 to 8.7 percent, HR 20.3 to 37 percent (hint). The 29 percent (8/28) and 50 percent (14/28) quoted in the paper are Gick and Holyoak 1983 Exp 2, cited by the authors, not their own result.
limits: One model (GPT-4, 2024), a single prompt per cell, 15 runs. The 'used the analogy' label is self-report by the model. The model sometimes claims an analogy it may not have used (demand effect). Authors suggest causal checks as future work.
agent_relevance: Gap 10. Resolves the c16 puzzle: 50 percent is the G&H 1983 hint figure, not a Puranam hint figure. Retrieval with a hint shows over-application: the agent must test the candidate source against the target's causal structure (G3) and may reject. Not yet tested.

source: Kurtz and Loewenstein (2007; 2004 proceedings version) Converging on a new role for analogy in problem solving and retrieval: when two problems are better than one
finding: Comparing two unsolved problems at test time, with an instruction to find one shared solution, produced the convergence solution as well as or better than comparing two solved stories at study time.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=293 students; cells 70 to 76): one story + one problem 13 percent; two stories compared at study 38 percent; one story then two problems compared 51 percent; two problems alone (no story) 25 percent. Chi-square: compare-targets vs baseline 24.06, p<.001; vs source comparison p=.11; vs just targets 10.58, p<.005; just targets vs baseline p=.06. Exp 2 (N=224): source comparison 35, target comparison 40, two problems without the shared-solution hint 16 percent (chi-square 10.77, p<.005).
limits: One problem family (radiation/convergence), paper packets, students, scoring by one rater blind to condition. The result needs an explicit instruction to find a common solution; two problems solved separately gave 16 percent, near baseline. Same research group as the other comparison work. This is the conference-proceedings text of the paper; the 2007 journal numbers were not separately checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 3. A new operator candidate: when stuck on one problem, write a sibling problem with the same structure and solve both under one shared-strategy instruction. Needs an LLM test. Also a boundary condition: comparison must be directed.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models (re-opened)
finding: Replication of Webb et al. holds, but on altered versions of simple letter-string, digit-matrix and story problems the GPT models drop where humans do not. Which change matters differs by domain.
numbers: Digit matrices, GPT-4 (0613): original digits 0.813, blank in alternate position 0.480, symbols instead of digits 0.790 (humans stayed flat across all three). Story analogies: GPT-4 was 89 percent (16/18) accurate when the correct answer was Story A but 61 percent (11/18) when it was Story B. Paraphrasing the correct target also hurt GPT-4 more than humans. Letter-string: humans flat across alphabet variants at zero generalisations, GPT models fell sharply, most for symbol alphabets. Human N=245 for stories on Prolific.
limits: GPT-3, 3.5 and GPT-4 (2023 versions); no reasoning-trained models. Table 1 text layout is garbled, so only the digit-matrix and story numbers are quoted. Symbol swap alone did not hurt on digit matrices (0.79 vs 0.81), so the surface-form effect is not uniform.
agent_relevance: Gap 5. Stored abstractions may not survive renamed symbols or a moved blank on weaker models, but the damage depends on which feature changes. A rewording or normalisation step before applying a stored rule is cheap and testable. No current reasoning model was tested here.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Changing only names in grade-school maths problems barely moves accuracy, changing numbers moves it more, and adding one irrelevant clause (GSM-NoOp) causes large drops even for the strongest reasoning model tested.
numbers: GSM-NoOp accuracy drop: o1-preview -17.5 points; weaker models up to 65 percent (Phi-3-mini). Names-only change: small drop and lower variance than number changes. 8 shots of the same question, with the irrelevant clause shown, did not remove the drop (stayed within one standard deviation). GPT-4o showed a negligible gap between GSM8K and GSM-Symbolic; several small models dropped more (contamination suspected).
limits: Maths word problems, a perturbation of content, not a re-coding of the rule. o1-preview is the only reasoning model in the headline NoOp result. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5. Even a reasoning-trained model loses about 17 points when a surface distractor sits in the target. A stored rule is only safe if the application step checks relevance of each clause. Pairs with the target-wording rescue idea.

source: Zhang, Madaan, Gao et al. (2024) In-Context Principle Learning from Mistakes (LEAP)
finding: The model solves its own few-shot examples, compares its wrong answers with the right ones, writes explicit lessons, and uses the lessons at test time. This is an LLM version of induction by comparing cases, here wrong against right.
numbers: Same 3 to 6 labelled examples as the baseline. GPT-4: +7.5 points on DROP and +3.3 on HotpotQA over few-shot CoT. Math (GPT-4): GSM8K 93.6 to 94.2 and MATH 63.5 to 64.5 across the three variants, a spread under one point. In 37 of 42 task-by-model cells one LEAP variant beat the baseline; in 24 both did; in 3 neither. Llama-2-chat-70B: no gain even when GPT-4 wrote the principles, because it did not follow them.
limits: 2023 to early 2024 models. Prompts are longer than baseline, so tokens are not equal. Table text is garbled, so which variant is which on math was not verified. Principles are made once per task, not per instance. Gain is largest where errors are knowledge or reading errors.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 3. Nearest LLM test of comparing cases to derive a rule: gains are real on reading and QA, close to zero on strong-model math, and zero on models that cannot follow the rule. A wrong-versus-right contrast already exists for LLMs, so the statement that there is no LLM contrast work needs this exception.

source: Chia et al. (2023) Contrastive Chain-of-Thought Prompting
finding: Showing both a valid and an invalid reasoning chain for each demonstration improves GPT-3.5-Turbo over standard chain of thought on arithmetic and factual QA.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo (0301). GSM8K: CoT 69.2, contrastive CoT 79.0 (+9.8). AQuA 53.5 to 57.5 (+4.0). With self-consistency the gains are +12.6 to +17.6 points over standard prompting across tasks. At least one task (SVAMP or ASDIV, row garbled) shows no gain or a small loss for contrastive CoT without self-consistency.
limits: Demonstration lengths double with the invalid chain, so tokens are not equal. Older model. Table text is garbled; only GSM8K and AQuA rows were checked. Invalid chains are made automatically by shuffling objects, so they are one narrow kind of near-miss.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. Contrast pairs (valid vs invalid) help LLMs on arithmetic at the cost of more tokens. A near-miss contrast arm for S2 is a testable cheap variant.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (re-opened for number of exemplars and model scale)
finding: Self-generated exemplars: one exemplar is worst, three to five are stable. The method helps large models, and small models do better with retrieved labelled examples.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo. Number of self-generated exemplars K=1 to 5: GSM8K 76.1, 77.0, 77.5, 77.3, 77.8; MATH 34.8, 36.7, 37.3, 37.0, 37.1. So K=1 to K=3 is +1.4 on GSM8K and +2.5 on MATH. At smaller scale (text-curie-001, text-davinci-001) few-shot with labelled examples beat self-generation; at text-davinci-002 and 003 self-generation won. Knowledge plus exemplars helped on Codeforces.
limits: Older models. The exemplar count is within-method (self-generated), not a human-style comparison of two given cases. Gains of 1 to 3 points on test sets of about 1000 problems may be near noise.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. Confirms K=1 is worst and that more than 3 adds little. Also shows self-generated cases only work when the model already knows the domain.

source: Boyce, Mathur, Frank (2023) Eleven years of student replication projects (as listed in the FORRT replication atlas for Gick and Holyoak 1983)
finding: The atlas lists one replication of Gick and Holyoak (1983), marked successful. It says adding the verbal statement helped transfer from a pair of analogs, as in the original. The atlas page gives no sample size or effect size.
numbers: Atlas entry: 1 replication, 1 successful, 2023. No N, no percentages on the page. The underlying data is in the Boyce et al. project data, which was not opened (journal page returned 403; Europe PMC search did not find it).
limits: Student replication projects are small and variable in quality. Success criterion not stated on the page. The earlier note b20 is therefore only half-resolved: author and direction confirmed, numbers still missing. The page was read through a summarising fetch tool, not as raw text.
agent_relevance: Gap 8. Direction agrees with the original for the pair-plus-statement effect. Treat as weak confirmation only.

source: Lewin (2026) Missing Skill or Failed Conceptual Control? A Behavior-Analytic Diagnosis of Language Model Failures on Counterfactual Analogy Problems (Zenodo preprint, abstract page only)
finding: Abstract says models do well on the standard alphabet and much worse on a permuted alphabet. Models name the next letter in the permuted alphabet almost perfectly, but GPT-4 rarely identifies the interval between two letters. Failures are framed as a missing component skill or a failure to combine skills that work alone.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page. Models other than GPT-4 not named.
limits: Abstract only, a single-author preprint on Zenodo, not peer reviewed. Includes no reasoning-trained models by name. Read through a summarising fetch tool.
agent_relevance: Gap 5. Suggests the failure is a component skill (interval in a new alphabet), so a rescue should rebuild that skill step by step rather than only rewording. Unverified; do not rely on it.
